problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=3{y}^{′}-2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=3,f(t)=-2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(2-3)f(t) \\  & =-f(t) \\  & =2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
